facts.statement: The study analyzed brain scans from 295 older adults who were part of the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers measured the density and cross-sectional area of three different groups of nerve fibers in each small region of the brain's white matter.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The cross-sectional area of the less dominant nerve fiber groups shrank the fastest as the participants got older.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: People with mild cognitive impairment had smaller cross-sectional areas in these less dominant fiber groups compared to those without cognitive issues.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: A larger cross-sectional area in these specific fiber groups was linked to better performance on executive function tasks.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The pattern of age-related decline in these fibers was consistent regardless of how many different fiber bundles crossed in a specific area, suggesting the fiber type itself drives the aging effect.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The study suggests that measuring fiber cross-section is a more reliable indicator of brain changes in complex areas than measuring fiber density.
facts.subject: humans
